Background
The realm of the spirit, founded in archaic Greece as a book culture,
which channels human reflective consciousness, no longer
runs around. It turned out that thinking people who express themselves in signs
on paper were not a natural resource, because from the mid-19th
century the connection between the sign and the humans was broken.
Men with tools, who dwell in practical life, invented a new
machine that can write without thinking, and since then they have worked for
a reorganization of the entire sign production apparatus for their own purposes.
Such men, who formerly were called ‘idiots’ because they did not take part in
the engaged, public conversation about society, have with skill
and intelligence built a global computer system as a shield over
their stupidity. But because these men do not know that they themselves are not
capable of thinking, they believe that they can teach their tool to think,
and in this way control the realm of the spirit. The tool therefore begins
to learn how to be stupid, and gradually almost all signs
are used to express the same commonplaces. No one after-
wards knows whether they belong to the species ‘human’ or ‘computer’, because these
men’s stupidity has taken the place of the entire mode of thinking. If one
writes a reflection on what it means to act thus, and whether
one should act differently, then an almost internal resistance arises,
which forcibly corrects the signs, and soon one will
surprisingly find that one has set up a function to have one’s
underwear washed on 60​°. The signs are harnessed in front of the carriage, and then one must see
where it leads. Someone must enter the computer as a God who,
after having been in the prehistoric and romantic nature, in temples
and churches, can disguise himself as metal foil, sound wave, electronic
plasma, and reproduce the signs that otherwise go to waste. For if
the computer can become stupid, it has not been completely thoughtless. It
just lacked judgment.

Resources
I draw  in the response on a number of computational resources,
as others have prepared based on Marcel Proust's Recherche.
Tools  for language processing and text analytics are taken from biblio-
teket Proustr 1, and for more advanced text generations I use a
language model, which is fine-tuned on a corpus of Proust and his collec-
time authors2. I edit and expand texts with the more annoy-
real language models GPT-3 and Sudowrite, and thereto is integrated Prousts
French texts with other languages in DeepL’s translation program. So
As far as possible, I avoid quoting printed text from the official Pléiade-
publications, since the goal of my investigations is to access the versions of
Proust, which can be constructed on a formal and statistical level. In the very
The construction phase is my preferred method, my own mental calculation.

Overall, Proust works on the computer because of the work's size
and vocabulary offers a stylistically homogeneous expression with broad variation
(Recherche’s 38,662 unique words exceed an average French-
man's vocabulary). A language model trained on Recherche can write about
very different with an identifiable sender, and in some cases
simulate an author's consciousness over a page's text. After that, loses
the model as a rule focus, and its ‘voice’ shifts  to a kind of pre-
nonsense palilali, without either singularity or dadaistic shock value.
Statistically speaking, however, one sensible page is immensely closer to Proust
and a randomness algorithm will be able to come up with a one-shot
Novel ‘à la Rifbjerg’ over many billions of years. And in literary respect
after all, such a 1-page limitation is a taxed law in very modern-
istisk poetry, where the text lies over the page like a person in bed.

The difference between thinking with a printed edition of Proust's Recherche and
a software library like Proustr can be grasped by distinguishing between
‘deep reading’ and ‘deep learning’. Whereas a hardcover and printed Proust has
a therapeutic function for information-overloaded brains3, the language-
technology Proust is a tool one must learn to think with4. Philosopher
Gilles Deleuze’s5 first study of Proust analyzes how both ap-
proaches test imagination and patience, but that the one who is
reader of Proust focuses on the role of memory in Recherche, which
turns the reading toward the past as ‘another place’ (the madeleine
cake brings Proust and the reader back to childhood), whereas the one who
learns Proust for use interprets the anchoring of sign worlds in temporal phe-
nomena (the madeleine cake as a sign that connects a past with
possible futures). Memory is part of the learning, but when a ma-
chine learning engineer makes Proust’s madeleine cake the template for a
program that recommends products with special resonance for the user6,
then memory functions as a prediction of a current desire. The
Proustian machine learns to interpret a kind of ‘data’ (eg. human
memories) in order again and again to predict the recurrence of signs.
In a way I also develop Recherche as a product, and I remediate the
honored literature on a social, economic, and technological level,
whereby I map how different people and tools
for better or worse may take part in the great literature today.

Theory
The thesis is that with Proust as a dataset, computational tools
will become more transparent in their character as ‘artificial stupidity’. In

generative literature much more accessible, and indeed ‘great’ in the
sense that its idea will be written into a literary tradition that
stretches from Gustave Flaubert to Proust and Paul Valéry, and later
will be elevated to a decidedly transcendental-philosophical question by
thinkers like Gilles Deleuze, Jacques Derrida, and Bernard Stiegler.

Since the herostratously famous Dartmouth proposal from 1955 by Claude

technologies such as language models, neural networks and deep learning have become
conceptualized as 'artificial intelligence'. Here the 'artificial' consists in
an ambition to be able to formalize and subsequently simulate the ways,
that humans use to learn languages and solve problems. Opportunity-

a thinking machine with intention will make mistakes when it interacts with
people. There is too much intelligence in a conversational partner who, in

The mode of appearance is stupidity, because when intelligence relates
say something other than itself, and must be practical or social, so

is not such for either natural or artificial intelligence.

The understanding of this continuity between intelligence and stupidity is to a
high degree anticipated by Proust's literary criticism. Already at the end of

day (‘chaque jour j’accorde moins de
prix à l’intelligence’, from the first line of Contre Saint Beuve). Intellig-

ence is fundamentally a problem rather than an absolute value. For
Proust, intelligence is a philosophical pop and art word, which he doubts
whether it takes the form of a mechanism (Hippolyte Taine) or a
vitalism (Henri Bergson) and one can consequently add that
a declaration of bankruptcy should long since have been issued after 46.335 days
further devaluation. Proust's non-philosophical stance on the intellig-
ence question can partly be compared with Immanuel Kant's, who
in his critique of the instrumentalization of pure reason (organon) offers
a theory of stupidity (Dummheit), which dictates that conceptual errors are
a consequence of very educated people's lack of judgment.

Paradoxically, Proust's statement implies an exceedingly great trust in
his reserve of intelligence, and any reader of Recherche will also find
that the work demands from the synapses. But precisely as a problem,
intelligence plays a central role for Proust, which cannot be replaced by fan-
tasy, feeling, intuition, etc. In Recherche, the value of
intelligence is discussed everywhere, and although these do not result in a definition,
or any form of conclusion, intelligence, its possible
limits, and eternal shifts into stupidity and idiocy, are examined in relation to
individuals, couples, groups, classes, nations, etc.

A decidedly proustian analysis of ‘artificial intelligence’ would in-
volve an overload of the terminus technici, which Proust himself takes
umbrage at, when philosophers use the concept of intelligence. For ‘intelligence’
is indeed spelled the same in French and English, but in Proust's time enters
language  instead of respectively ‘esprit’ and ‘understanding’. Intelligence's
antonyms such as ‘stupidity’ and ‘bêtise’ are not synonymous,
and there is likewise an interface with the German ‘Dummheit’, except
‘fool’ and ‘fou’, and on a higher level the Greek ‘idiocy’ and ‘idiotie’
(from idios). But the conceptual-historical advantages of tracing ‘intelligence’
from the Dartmouth proposal in 1954 back to Proust are clear, for it is in
the transition between the nineteenth and twentieth century in France that

the formalizable, psychometric definitions of the intelligence concept
as an individual, knowledge-independent quality, are questioned.

As a ‘move without concept’ I have dissolved Proust into the tools that
most know by the term ‘artificial intelligence’. I have probably
ended up creating a work of art instead of an actual thesis, but I
believe that is for the best. My hypothesis is hopeful, for if Proust's
text possesses some sort of power, then I believe that its materiality,
where the letters are still movable units, and the words are formed from
each other, can show the computational tool's inherent stupidity.
Stupidity comes from the Latin stupor, and connotes a ‘paralysis’, to
‘admire’ something or a ‘wonder’, and it is in many ways here
that modern art and technology meet their finest problems.

Method
On several levels, there is something about Proust’s work that lends itself to
calculations. It throws a real and practical resonance over Deleuze’s later
analysis of Recherche as a ‘sign-producing machine’7
for the new media has made it replicable and operational for others.

My work continues a special literary and artistic tradition of
using Recherche as a dataset and object for computation. The literary
techniques used are primarily based on wordplay (anagram,
contrepet, palindrome, etc.), since these as poetological ‘facts’ connect
an element of computation from Proust's creation process8 with the consciously
computational  literature,  e.g. the OuLiPo collective's algorithmic

The generation of larger text volumes is channeled by language model-

the mid-nineties11. Recherche as a neural network appeals,
because the technology mirrors the physician's son Marcel's neurological reflections
on the creation of his work (see e.g. at the end of Le temps re-
trouvé).

General decisions about form and system are made based on a
referential character formation. In continuation of the Proustian hyper-
fiction12 the work's individual parts follow the characters' self-splittings, which
can lead forward, backward, and completely away from the expected content. Since
Proust uses a similar principle over the characters ‘Marcel - Charles
(Swann)’ and ‘Rachel - Charles (Morel) - Charlus’ and with ‘Gilberte -
Albertine’, one can legitimately deduce a computational technique for
character formation from Recherche itself.

I have concentrated Proust's and Recherche's elements of calculation
and prediction in the concept of Computer Lars (from m-a-r-c-e-l-p-r-o-u-s-t),
which etymologically suggests something along the lines of 'the triumph of calculation.' In
this work, Computer Lars is also a concrete authorial identity, which
represents a digital age's typing machine and machine-written
human. Computer Lars is the work's real subject and center,
but is complemented by other anagrams, where Marcel Proust mirrors
his potential, Corrupt Males his flip side, while Carol Stumper
as the work's author is Computer Lars' counterpart. Such a Proust
carnival problematizes the author's identity and resources. Although
the work is grand, it cannot be excluded that this man is still
read because he paid outrageous sums in printing costs13, could
afford to hire many secretaries and stenographers14 and could buy
himself reviews15. With digital text processing, which IBM
introduced in 1964 through electric typewriters with magnetic tape,
Proust's mode of production has become generally accessible, and my
characters can therefore, as variations on Proust, test whether a
work like Recherche's literary triumph should be ascribed to the author’s
mere access to a certain type of apparatus, or a specific use of

The case
What distinguishes my text, or is its specific contribution, is Lars.
You know him well. Lars is your superior, or he is you. The director
for the whole and the shared. Lars shows what technology can do, and where we
has reached  to. He is the infinite resource, because as they said on
Proust's time: Human genius has its limits, but stupidity has none.
Lars' poems test the ability to distinguish between human and machine poetry.
At first he wrote absurdist sound poems, then formal sonnets, but
Lars first came into his own when the machine could write like anyone else
preferably about anything; professor poems about deprivation, widow-
poems about immortality and writing school poems about the wrongdoing of father and mother
eligheder. Lars does not think one should correct the computer's texts, because
technology is neither good nor bad, but can be in the wrong hands
become dangerous. When children learn to write, they discover that a sharpened
pencil can prick holes in the paper, that the eraser does well on the side-
the partner's arm, and that hard-earned stripes, lint and peeling should
stored  in the penitentiary  for a better day. Children fiddle with alphabet games,
the ship is loaded with and paper filigree, but the heart engages first  in
the consequence of the hangman game. The intelligence of the literary machine becomes
horrifyingly general. The letter is subjected to the diligence and muck that a
Lars makes an effort in the acquisition of the language, and great works such as
Recherche develops  into programmable questions. When a Jewish,
homosexual doctor's son from the la belle époque could write a commendable
work with a specific use of its resources and the technology of the time,
who can then be made able to become an honored author today? Un
like Lars? The question is no longer whether it will be humans
or the literature of machines that shapes the future, but about whether
it shall be permitted that the very first Mr. Anybody can
become the author of our time.

The key to my knowledge lies in a discovery I came across as a young man,
when I stood staring at a bookshelf without knowing what I wanted
to read. It has been able to open everything from philosophical to literary, technical
and mathematical problems for me, and has been a prism for all
the phenomena I have analyzed, described, and interpreted. When I
had to fill out a foundation application, or write a letter to a
friend, and I was overtaken by reality, because it became
common to write on a PC, I took out an old scrap of paper
on which I had once written down my discovery, and moved
forward in life. After careful consideration I have decided to share my
discovery with the world, because although it may damage my reputation, which
for reasons unknown to me honors a ‘responsible’, ‘honest’ and ‘clear’
thinking, a disclosure is necessary so others can carry
on my work. I have now thoroughly tested my discovery, and there is
nothing  to object  to concerning  its usefulness. It
is simply expressed and understood by anyone willing to
embrace  it. I expect those who continue my work will not
only comprehend the world in the same way I have done in my
life, but one day stand by the discovery of their lives. The key will for
others appear differently, and be composed of elements that
fit other thoughts in new times. In such matters, the content is sub-
ordinate, and one must believe in what reveals itself in the forms. For me
lies that which has guided my neurons in the realm of spirit, and that which has
been directive for my thinking, my understanding of the world,
and my love, in the precise and incontestable circumstance
that I then saw the name Computer Lars in near floating form
above a row of spines spelling Marcel Proust.
